Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) is a multisystem disease involving sclerotic, vascular, and inflammatory changes of the skin and internal organs such as lungs, heart, GI tract, and kidneys. There are 2 main types: diffuse systemic scleroderma (progressive systemic sclerosis—dSSc) and limited systemic scleroderma (limited systemic sclerosis—lSSc).Diffuse scleroderma involves the kidneys, heart, GI tract, and lungs, whereas limited scleroderma tends to spare these vital organs.
CREST syndrome (CS) defined by calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysfunction, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias, characteristics of limited scleroderma.
19.3 new cases per million adults per year in the United States (95% CI, 12.4-30.2).
Prevalence is estimated at 276 cases per million adults in the United States (95% CI, 245-310).
Female to male ratio is 4.6:1.
Mean age at diagnosis was not different for female and male patients (46.0 ± 15.8 years vs. 46.7 ± 16.9 years).
Autoimmune.
African-American patients are twice as likely as nonblack patients to have diffuse disease (OR 1.86, 95% CI, 1.48-2.35).

Silica exposure is associated with increased risk of systemic sclerosis (OR 2.8, 95%CI 1.9–4.2). Chemical solvent exposure (dry cleaning, paint thinners, chemical industry) is also associated with SSc (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.3–3.0). Silicone breast implants, epoxy resins, and pesticides have loose associations that are not significant.

Scleroderma is an autoimmune disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and vascular injury in the skin and other visceral organs. Although the pathogenesis remains unclear, interactions among leukocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts are likely to be central to the pathogenesis of the disease.

The diagnosis of systemic scleroderma requires the presence of the lone major criterion (proximal scleroderma) or 2 minor criteria (sclerodactyly, digital pitting scars or a loss of substance from finger pads, or bibasilar pulmonary fibrosis). C

list.listitem: summarizes the American College of Rheumatology preliminary criteria for the diagnosis of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).
The 2013 ACR EULAR criteria for the diagnosis of systemic sclerosis are shown in .
See for characteristics of limited and diffuse scleroderma.

Sclerodactyly is the tightness, thickening, and nonpitting induration involving the fingers and toes. Although it is almost always present in patients with proximal scleroderma, its presence is not sufficient to make the diagnosis of systemic scleroderma.

Proximal scleroderma is the tightening, thickening, and nonpitting induration affecting the skin proximal to the metacarpophalangeal or metatarsophalangeal joints as well as other areas, such as: extremities, face, neck, or trunk (thorax or abdomen). It is usually bilateral and symmetrical and can also include sclerodactyly.
Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by cold exposure leading to the blanching of digits, followed by blue and red color. It is seen in most patients with scleroderma.
Breathlessness is the chief symptom of interstitial lung disease associated with systemic sclerosis (SSc-ILD).
CREST syndrome is calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysfunction, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias, characteristics of limited scleroderma.
The sensitivity of the ACR criteria increased from 67% to 99% with the addition of nail-fold capillary abnormalities identified using a dermatoscope and the presence of visible telangiectasias.

Because of the presence of ANA in normal patients and its absence in afflicted patients, ANA test results must be interpreted within the clinical context. In a case-control study comparing patients with known scleroderma and healthy controls, ANA was 95% sensitive and 87% specific for scleroderma at a 1:80 dilution (LR+ 7.3, LR− 0.06). However, this type of study is likely to overestimate the accuracy of ANA because of "spectrum bias" (including only healthy and known diseased patients rather than patients with a more appropriate spectrum, such as suspected collagen vascular disease).
Anticentromere antibody (ACA) predicts limited skin involvement, whereas antitopoisomerase I antibody (Scl-70) predicts diffuse skin involvement with lung disease.

In a large meta-analysis that included 30 studies, ACA was positive in 32% of patients with dSSc and 57% of those with ISSc, while Scl-70 was positive in 34% of patients with ISSc and 40% of those with dSSc.
ACA was present in 5% and Scl-70 in 2% of patients with other connective tissue diseases, but less than 1% of disease-free controls had either antibody present.
Apply the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) diagnostic criteria ().
Once the disease is diagnosed, use to classify whether the patient has limited systemic scleroderma or diffuse systemic scleroderma.
Recommended initial lab tests include ANA, CBC, ESR, BUN and Cr, UA, chest x-ray, and pulmonary function tests.
If ANA is positive, test for the following autoantibodies: ACA and Scl-70.
Skin biopsy is recommended to confirm scleroderma if the clinical picture is unclear.
Treatment is mainly supportive and symptomatic, targeting patient specific disease manifestations (see ). C
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and PDE-5 inhibitors are moderately effective in secondary Raynaud's phenomenon resulting from scleroderma. A

Rituximab is a safe and effective treatment for SSc-ILD with improved lung function compared to cyclophosphamide, and improved skin thickness with fewer adverse effects. B
Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHSCT) is a therapeutic option for patients with severe systemic sclerosis., B
Treatment is mainly supportive and symptomatic, targeting whichever specific organs affect the patient (see ).
Management of pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with systemic sclerosis (SSc-PAH) is in consensus with CHEST guidelines, but studies are limited, as few address SSc-PAH specifically.
Endothelin antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan) improve time to clinical progression and exercise capacity in patients with PAH.

PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) improve exercise capacity and reduce risk of clinical worsening in a heterogenous patient population, some with connective tissue disease-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension (CTD-PAH).
Riociguat (soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator) improves time to clinical worsening and exercise capacity in a heterogenous study population including patients with SSc-PAH.

Continuous intravenous epoprostenol should be considered in patients with severe SSc-PAH. A RCT involving 111 patients with SSc-PAH indicated that epoprostenol, along with conventional therapy, improved the median 6 minute walk test distance, NYHA functional class, and Borg dyspnea index.

A 2018 Cochrane Review demonstrated low quality evidence that cyclophosphamide may provide small, clinically significant improvement in FVC when compared to placebo, but no difference in carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (DLCO) or impact on mortality. Cyclophosphamide had no significant impact on lung function when compared to mycophenolate, but had increased risk of side effects including thrombocytopenia and leukopenia.

Mycophenolate showed improvement in DLCO, breathlessness score, forced vital capacity percent predicted when compared to placebo in a 2024 systematic review. When compared to cyclophosphamide, there was no difference in quality of life, mortality, or disease progression. There were fewer adverse events with mycophenolate versus cyclophosphamide. A 2021 systematic review demonstrated comparable efficacy of mycophenolate to cyclophosphamide in regards for FVC and DLCO in patients with SSc-ILD. Mycophenolate had less adverse effects and is overall preferable given comparable efficacy.

Rituximab is a safe and effective alternative to cyclophosphamide in the treatment of pulmonary and skin manifestations of dSSc. In a randomized control trial, patients treated with rituximab had an improvement in FVC compared to cyclophosphamide, and also had improved skin thickness on the modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS) with fewer adverse effects. A meta-analysis demonstrated improvement in FVC and DLCO at 1 year in patients treated with rituximab when compared with controls. The study also showed a trend towards reduced infectious complications when compared to other immunosuppressants. A 2023 systematic review and meta analysis of 3 studies of rituximab showed improvement in modified Rodnan Skin Score and forced vital capacity percent of predicted at 24-48 weeks.

In a double-blind randomized control trial, nintedanib (Ofev) reduced the decline of FVC compared to placebo in patients with SSc-ILD, though did not affect mRSS at 1 year. The reduction in FVC was seen in patients with SSc-ILD who were and were not concurrently taking mycophenolate. Nintedanib had similar adverse effects with and without mycophenolate, and the side effect profile is similar to the previously known drug profile in other ILD populations.

Nintedanib and nintedanib + mycophenolate combination both demonstrated a reduction in FVC decline in a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis, but with an increased risk of gastrointenstinal adverse effects and discontinuation when compared to placebo. The quality of evidence was not high.

Toclizumab demonstrated a smaller percentage decrease in forced vital capacity, DLCO percentage, and modified Rodnan skin Scores when compared to placebo in a systematic review and meta-analysis involving 5 studies. It may have an increased role in treatment of SSc-ILD.

Early treatment with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor may improve prognosis in scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). In a prospective review of 108 patients with SRC, patients on ACE inhibitors had significantly improved 1 and 5 year mortality that persisted after adjustment for age and blood pressure.
ACE inhibitors are not recommended for prevention to decrease the development of SRC. The use of ACE inhibitors before SRC is associated with poorer prognosis and an increased likelihood of SRC.

A 2017 Cochrane Review found calcium channel blockers (CCBs), particularly dihydropyridine class, have low to moderate quality evidence in reducing the duration, severity, frequency, pain, and disability associated with Raynaud’s phenomenon.

A 2023 Cochrane review demonstrated that PDE5 inhibitors may slightly reduce frequency and duration of Raynaud’s phenomenon per week. They did not demonstrate an improvement in pain but did improve patient’s global assessment of their disease. There were no significant differences in adverse effects between treatment groups.

Compared with placebo, nifedipine modestly reduces the severity and frequency of Raynaud's ischemic attacks (i.e., average of 3 to 5 fewer attacks per week and 33% reduction in severity of attacks). Use 10 to 30 mg three times daily or the long-acting form starting at 30 mg daily. Slowly titrate the dose upward to relieve symptoms.

PDE-5 inhibitors improve frequency, severity, and duration of attacks secondary to Raynaud’s phenomenon. The medication class has increased side effects compared to CCBs and should be considered in patients who do not respond to CCBs.
Losartan reduced the frequency and severity of Raynaud's phenomenon in a nonblinded RCT compared with a low dose of nifedipine.

Intravenous iloprost reduces the severity and frequency of SSc-associated Raynaud’s phenomenon, including ischemic attacks and Raynaud’s Phenomenon severity score when compared with placebo. Given the route of administration, they should be considered after CCBs and PDE-5 inhibitors.

A 2013 meta-analysis indicated that PDE-5 inhibitors significantly improved healing of digital ulcers (RR 3.3, 95% CI 1.3-8.1), although analysis was limited by study heterogeneity. Bosentan reduced the average number of new digital ulcers (standardized mean difference -0.34, 95% CI -0.57, -0.11). IV iloprost prevented new digital ulcers (SMD 0.77, 95% CI -1.5, -0.08).

A 2023 meta-analysis involving 469 patients with diffuse and limited SSc treated with bosentan demonstrated a decrease in number of new digital ulcers when compared to placebo (WMD: -0.89 [95% CI: -1.40, -0.37; P = 0.001]) and improvement in Rodnan skin score, mean SSc-Health Questionnaire Assessment, and pain.

Methotrexate can be considered for management of skin manifestations in early diffuse SSc. In a RCT of 73 patients, oral methotrexate decreased the UCLA skin score and mRSS when compared with placebo.

Intravenous iloprost reduced the number of digital ulcers when compared with placebo in a small RCT. Complete healing of all cutaneous lesions was observed at 10 weeks in 85% of treatment group compared to 0% of placebo (p=0.015).

Botulinum toxin B (BTX-B) may be of benefit for patients with digital ulcers. A small RCT showed improved pain/numbness symptoms, reduction of new digital ulcers, and enhanced skin temperature recovery at 16 weeks. Further studies are needed given the limited size of this trial.

In a small RCT, both botulinum toxin A (BTX-A) and intravenous prostaglandins (iloprost/alprostadil) both improved digital ulcer healing and pain control. BTX-A was a more rapid treatment modality (compared to IV infusion) and significantly more cost effective.
An uncontrolled series of 8 patients with calcinosis unresponsive to previous treatment reported an apparent response to rituximab in 4 of the patients.

A 2019 Cochrane review on morphea concluded that oral methotrexate (MTX) and oral prednisone might improve disease manifestations compared to placebo and prednisone in juvenile active morphea (generalized or mixed morphea, linear, circumscribed, and linear scleroderma). A higher risk of adverse effects was seen in the combination treatment group. There was no significant difference in outcomes for adults and children with active morphea with UVA-1 and UVB on skin damage or disease. These conclusions were based on low quality evidence.

A systematic review concluded that UVB is effective for superficial lesions while UVA is better for deeper lesions. Methotrexate and corticosteroids are also useful for more severe disease. Calcipotriene and tacrolimus are helpful as topical agents for limited lesions. A review of the evidence does not support the use of oral calcipotriol, antimalarial drugs, interferon, or d-penicillamine.

A single arm trial evaluated of mycophenolate in 61 patients poorly responsive to standard therapy including MTX. After 9 to 12 months , 47 of 14 patients had stable disease, 33 had improved disease activity, and 27 achieved remission.
Debridement, amputation, and grafts may be needed for ischemic digital ulcers.
Contractures that limit function may require surgical release.
Excision can relieve painful calcinotic nodules.

Telangiectases in patients with systemic sclerosis can be treated with pulsed dye laser or intense pulsed light. The former has somewhat better cosmetic outcomes, while the latter has fewer adverse effects ()
Physical and occupational therapy may be needed to maintain range of motion and delay contractures.

Exercise programs are beneficial for improvement in physical performance and functional capacity in patients with diffuse systemic sclerosis. A 2021 randomized control trial comparing supervised exercise programs with home exercise programs demonstrated benefit for improvement in functional capacity with each intervention. Both groups had statistically significant improvements in 6 minute walk test, Hehlth Rerated Quqlity of Lile, and fatigue. The suparticipants in the pervised exercise program dealso monstrated improvement in pulmonary function and dyspnea severity, that was not seen in home exercise program. Another small RCT (n=44) demonstrated statistically significant improvement in 6-minute walk test, strength (hand grip, biceps, quadriceps), disability, and quality of life in a minimally supervised home exercise program compared to placebo over 6 months.

A mobile-app based occupational therapy intervention was similar to intensive (in person) occupational therapy on QuickDASH (functional scoring for Diseases of Arm, Shoulder, Hand) in a small pilot trial for patients with dSSc. The mobile-app group showed sustained improvements over the 18 week study, while intensive group had greater initial gains and then lost over time in functionality scored on the QuickDASH.
Raynaud's flare-ups may be prevented by avoiding cold temperatures and not smoking.
Smoking should be avoided in all patients with scleroderma to prevent further complications of Raynaud's phenomenon and lung disease. C

Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHSCT) may be a therapeutic option for patients with severe systemic sclerosis. A 2022 Cochrane review demonstrated moderate certainty evidence that non-myeloablative hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and myeloablative selective HSCT showed improvement in skin thickness and event-free survival when compared to cyclophosphamide. Two studies with non-myeloablative HSCT patients demonstrated improvement in forced vital capacity, skin scores, and safety – though with low certainty evidence. There was an increased risk of adverse events of HSCT when compared to cyclophosphamide including early treatment related mortality and other complications. A 2023 meta-analysis of 22 studies echoed these findings with improvement in lung function and skin thickness score, but with higher treatment related deaths when compared with cyclophosphamide. A 2020 systematic review demonstrated durable statistically significant improvement in health related quality of life in patients with severe systemic sclerosis post-AHSCT. A careful risk assessment should be performed when considering HSCT for SSc.,,

Consider referral and/or hospitalization for patients with renal failure (acute or chronic ), malignant hypertension, severe wound infections secondary to infarctions, symptomatic chronic severe interstitial lung disease, or heart failure.

Complications include renal failure (acute or chronic), malignant hypertension, severe wound infections secondary to infarctions, symptomatic pulmonary hypertension, severe interstitial lung disease, or heart failure. See corresponding chapters for details on managing these complications.
About 70% of patients with limited systemic scleroderma survive 10 years compared with only 21% of patients with diffuse systemic scleroderma. B
Monitor patients for complications such as pulmonary hypertension, interstitial lung disease, renal failure, malignant hypertension, or heart failure. C
Prognosis depends on subtype and organs affected.

Systemic sclerosis has higher mortality than the general population with a Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR) 2.823, (95% CI 2.219–3.591, p<0.001). The overall SMR does not depend on geographical region or sex. SMR was increased in diffuse SSc (SMR 4.865, 95% CI 3.863–6.127, p<0.001) compared with limited SSc (SMR 2.020, 95% CI 1.570–2.599, p<0.001).
Seventy-one percent of patients with limited cutaneous scleroderma survive 10 years compared with 21% of patients with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma.
Prediction models such as the Du Bois index and Composite Physiologic Index developed for patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis have good predictive validity.

Prognosis worsens with renal, pulmonary, or cardiac involvement; pulmonary disease is the leading cause of death. Predictors of mortality in 1 study were age 65 years or more at enrollment, FVC<50% predicted, clinically significant arrhythmia on EKG, absence of anticentromere antibodies, hypertension, chest radiograph suggestive of pulmonary fibrosis, and low body mass index (BMI); HLA alleles DRB1*0802 and DQA1*0501 were also significant predictors of mortality.

Survival in patients with systemic sclerosis associated pulmonary hypertension was 90% at 1 year (95% CI: 86-93%), 66% at 3 years (95% CI: 59-72%), and 44% at 5 years (95% CI: 23-65%) per a 2023 systematic review involving 530 patients. Risk factors associated with mortality included six minute walking distance, age, pericardial effusion, NYHA Classification, male gender, and pulmonary arterial pressure (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37398831/ ) A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that patients with SSc-PAH had an increased pooled mortality when compared to SSc patients without pulmonary hypertension.
In one study, 21% of patients with systemic sclerosis reported work disability; this increased with disease duration.

A systematic review of 6 studies with 6641 patients found that patients with scleroderma have an increased risk for cancer (standardized incidence ratio 1.4, 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). Lung cancer was especially common (SIR 3.2, 95% CI, 2.1-4.8).

Specific lung CT findings including extensive ILD, ILD extent, reticulation extent, ILD densitrometric analysis, and fibrotic extent were independent predictors of mortality in patients with SSc-ILD in a 2021 systematic review.

Data from Scleroderma Lung Studies I and II identified risk factors for increased mortality in SSc-ILD including older age, higher baseline mRSS, and decline of DLCO and FVC over two years. The decline of FVC and DLCO over two years was a more accurate indicator of mortality then baseline measurements.

Interstitial lung disease (ILD): Monitor patients with PFTs, DLCO, chest x-ray, and if needed high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan or bronchoalveolar lavage. Ultrasound indicating lung comets (echographic sign of interstitial fibrosis) in 1 study had a high correlation with HRCT (r=0.72); its role in diagnosis and monitoring ILD is unknown.
Pulmonary hypertension: Echocardiography is used to monitor patients with peripheral edema, dyspnea, and fatigue.

Renal crisis: Monitoring BP at each visit is important to evaluate for malignant hypertension. Renal function tests, peripheral smear, and UA are needed if renal crisis (characterized by microangiopathy, hemolytic anemia, renal insufficiency, and malignant hypertension) is suspected.
Dysphagia and GERD: Esophageal manometry, pH, barium swallow, or endoscopy may be needed if the patient is symptomatic.

Patients who become pregnant with systemic sclerosis are at higher risk of miscarriage (OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.2-2.2), low birth weight (OR 3.8, 95% CI 2.2-6.6), preterm birth (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1-4.9), or fetuses with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) (OR 3.2, 95% CI 2.2-4.5) compared with healthy controls. Patients with SSc were also at higher risk of Cesarean section (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.37-3.8) and developing gestational hypertension (OR 2.8, 95% CI 2.3-3.4).

A prospective Italian study followed 99 women with systemic sclerosis. After 10 years, they reported 109 pregnancies and 101 successful deliveries. IUGR was more common (6% vs 1% in general population) as was preterm birth (25% vs 12%) and more severe prematurity (10% vs 5%).
Systemic sclerosis is rare in children.

feature.caption: American College of Rheumatology Preliminary Criteria for the Diagnosis of Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma).
feature.feature_body:
The diagnosis of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) requires the presence of the lone major criterion OR two minor criteria. Major:
Proximal scleroderma: symmetric thickening, tightening, and nonpitting induration of the skin proximal to the metatarsophalangeal or metacarpophalangeal joints
Minor:
Sclerodactyly Digital pitting scars on fingertips or loss of substance of the distal finger pad Bilateral basilar pulmonary fibrosis
Data from Preliminary criteria for the classification of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). Subcommittee for scleroderma criteria of the American Rheumatism Association Diagnostic and Therapeutic Criteria Committee. Arthritis Rheum 1980;23:581-590.

feature.caption: Characteristics of Diffuse Systemic Sclerosis (Diffuse Scleroderma) and Limited Systemic Sclerosis (Limited Scleroderma).
feature.feature_body:
Diffuse Systemic Sclerosis (Diffuse Scleroderma) Limited Systemic Sclerosis (Limited Scleroderma)
Constitutional Fatigue, weight loss or gain No constitutional symptoms
Vascular Mild Raynaud's phenomenon Severe Raynaud's phenomenon
Cutaneous Sclerosis to trunk, arms, and face; rapidly progressive Sclerosis to hands or toes and face, slow progression; calcinosis prominent
Musculoskeletal Arthralgias and deformities, muscle weakness, and tendon friction rubs Joint stiffness
Gastrointestinal GERD, esophageal dysmotility, and malabsorption are common; may be severe Mild-to-moderate GERD and esophageal dysmotility common; malabsorption less common
Renal Severe hypertension and renal infarcts in renal crisis are common Rare
Pulmonary Pulmonary hypertension and interstitial lung disease are common Uncommon
Cardiac Cardiomyopathy, heart failure, and arrhythmias are common Uncommon
Data from LeRoy EC, Black C, Fleischmajer R, et al. Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis): classification, subsets and pathogenesis. J Rheumatol 1988;15:202-205.
